Research question: For a native macOS research/PKM app (Epistemos — sandboxed Mac App Store build, solo dev, Swift, URLSession networking only, NO server-side component except an optional small proxy, user keys stored in Keychain), which research-content sources can be integrated as first-class "ResearchHub" feed/bookmark features — the way the app already ingests arXiv via its open API — and what is the EXACT 2026 integration reality for each?

Sources to evaluate (verdict per source: official API? auth model (none/API-key/OAuth-PKCE)? price/tier as of mid-2026? rate limits? licensing/ToS constraints on displaying content? RSS/Atom fallback? MAS-sandbox-viable without a server? effort S/M/L):
1. X.com (Twitter) — SPECIFICALLY the Bookmarks endpoint (GET /2/users/:id/bookmarks): which paid tier unlocks it in 2026, OAuth 2.0 PKCE user-context requirements, free-tier reality, and ToS-safe alternatives if the API is unaffordable (official export? browser-extension export formats an app can import? does X have a native bookmarks export in 2026?).
2. Reddit — API terms/pricing 2026 for a free client app, OAuth, per-subreddit RSS/.json feeds as the sanctioned lightweight path.
3. Hacker News — official Firebase API + Algolia HN Search API (both free/no-auth?).
4. GitHub — REST API for starred repos/releases/notifications, token rate limits, Atom feeds, and the trending-page problem (no official API — what do apps use in 2026?).
5. Hugging Face — Hub API (models/datasets), Daily Papers API (huggingface.co/api/daily_papers), auth needs, papers-with-code status after HF absorbed it.
6. Scholarly beyond arXiv — Semantic Scholar API, OpenAlex, PubMed E-utilities, bioRxiv/medRxiv, Crossref, OpenReview API: auth/price/rate limits, which are best for a personal research app, Google Scholar's no-API reality.
7. Read-later/bookmark ecosystems — Raindrop.io API, Instapaper, Readwise Reader API, Zotero API (personal library sync), Pocket (confirm 2025 shutdown status and what replaced it), Are.na.
8. Fediverse/new social — Bluesky AT Protocol (public feeds + did it ship native bookmarks?), Mastodon API bookmarks endpoint, Lobsters JSON.
9. RSS/Atom as the universal fallback lane (blogs/Substack/YouTube channel feeds) and YouTube Data API quota reality.

Also research: (a) how comparable Mac/iOS apps architect multi-source research feeds legally (NetNewsWire, Reeder, Readwise Reader, Folo/Follow, Raycast extensions) — client-side-only vs proxy; (b) App Store review constraints on showing third-party content (attribution, NSFW filtering for Reddit, API-key entry UX); (c) whether any source REQUIRES a server middleman (secret can't live in the client) vs pure client-side OAuth PKCE.

Deliverable emphasis: a per-source verdict table (API status, auth, cost, MAS-viability, effort, worth-it ranking), the top-5 "build first" sources for a research-heavy app, the X-bookmarks decision specifically (API tier vs import-file fallback), and a recommended ResearchHub architecture (unified item schema → per-source adapters → save-to-vault), all with 2026-current citations. Prioritize official docs/pricing pages over blog posts; flag anything that changed in 2024-2026 (Reddit API pricing, X tiers, Pocket shutdown).

confirmed.claim: The X API v2 Bookmarks surface is live and documented on docs.x.com with five endpoints, including the read endpoint GET /2/users/:id/bookmarks plus bookmark-folder reads (GET /2/users/:id/bookmarks/folders and GET /2/users/:id/bookmarks/folders/:folder_id), so an app can retrieve both a user's bookmarks and their bookmark folders via the official API.
confirmed.quote: The Bookmarks endpoints let you view, add, and remove bookmarked Posts for the authenticated user.

confirmed.claim: Bookmarks access requires user-context authentication — user access tokens obtained via OAuth 2.0 PKCE (or 3-legged OAuth) — plus an approved developer account and a Project/App in the Developer Console; PKCE support means a public-client (no client secret) flow is officially supported, which matters for a sandboxed Mac app with no server.
confirmed.quote: An approved developer account, A Project and App in the Developer Console, User Access Tokens via OAuth 2.0 PKCE or 3-legged OAuth

confirmed.claim: This official Bookmarks introduction page states NO access-tier gating (Free/Basic/Pro/Enterprise), no pricing, and no rate limits — its complete prerequisites list omits any paid-tier requirement — so the crux question of which 2026 tier unlocks GET bookmarks cannot be answered from this page and must be verified against X's separate tier/pricing documentation.
confirmed.quote: An approved developer account, A Project and App in the Developer Console, User Access Tokens via OAuth 2.0 PKCE or 3-legged OAuth

confirmed.claim: As of mid-2026, the X API no longer uses subscription tiers (Free/Basic/Pro); it uses pay-per-usage credit pricing, so the research question's framing of 'which paid tier unlocks bookmarks' is obsolete — there are no tiers, only per-request credit costs.
confirmed.quote: The X API uses pay-per-usage pricing. No subscriptions—pay only for what you use.

confirmed.claim: Effective Monday, April 20, 2026, X prices the bookmarks endpoint GET /2/users/{id}/bookmarks (along with followers, following, liked_tweets, tweets, mentions, lists, blocking, muting endpoints) under 'Owned Reads' at $0.001 per resource returned, i.e., $1 per 1,000 bookmarks fetched — a usage-based model rather than a flat tier gate.
confirmed.quote: Starting Monday, April 20, 2026, these endpoints will be priced at $0.001 per resource (equivalently, 1,000 resources for $1): GET /2/users/{id}/bookmarks

confirmed.claim: X defines 'Owned Reads' as requests made by a developer's own app for that account's own data — explicitly including bookmarks — but the announcement does not explicitly state whether end-users authenticating into a third-party client app (OAuth user context) receive this rate, nor which subscription tier is prerequisite, deferring the complete rate card to the X API Pricing page.
confirmed.quote: Owned Reads are requests made by your own developer app for your own posts, bookmarks, followers, likes, lists & more.

confirmed.claim: twitter-web-exporter exports X/Twitter bookmarks (bypassing the 800-item cap) without using the official paid Twitter API or requiring a developer account — it works as a Tampermonkey/Violentmonkey userscript that passively captures the web app's own GraphQL responses, so a Mac app could rely on it as the export step in an import-file fallback for X bookmarks.
confirmed.quote: The script itself does not send any request to Twitter API. It installs an network interceptor to capture the response of GraphQL request

confirmed.claim: X's official native archive export does NOT include bookmarks (and represents following/followers only as numeric IDs), meaning there is no first-party bookmarks export from X and a third-party tool like this is required for an import-based workflow.
confirmed.quote: Twitter's archive only contains the numeric user ID of your following/followers which is not human-readable. The archive also does not contain your bookmarks.

refuted.claim: The Bookmarks read endpoint (GET /2/users/{id}/bookmarks) is classified as an 'Owned Read' priced at $0.001 per resource when an app fetches the authenticated user's own data — meaning a personal research app pulling a user's own 1,000 bookmarks would cost roughly $1, making X bookmarks integration financially viable for a solo-dev app.

unverified.claim: As of mid-2026, Reddit's free-access Data API rate limit is 100 queries per minute per OAuth client ID, averaged over a 10-minute window to permit bursting — ample for a personal research/PKM client's feed polling.

OAuth authentication is mandatory for the Reddit Data API: clients must use a registered OAuth token, and unauthenticated traffic is blocked outright rather than given a default rate limit — so a MAS client app must implement Reddit OAuth (or fall back to RSS) rather than hitting .json endpoints anonymously.

Free Data API access exists in 2026 but is framed as conditional eligibility governed by Reddit's Responsible Builder Policy, Developer Terms, and Data API Terms, with a 'contact us to request' step — there is no self-serve paid tier or pricing schedule published on this official wiki page.

Any app that persists Reddit content locally (e.g., Epistemos save-to-vault) has a ToS obligation to delete content and author-identifying data once it is deleted on Reddit — Reddit recommends purging stored user data within 48 hours and states that retaining deleted content even in anonymized form violates its terms.

Mastodon provides an official, documented API endpoint for reading a user's bookmarks: GET /api/v1/bookmarks, which returns the statuses the authenticated user has bookmarked as an array of Status entities.

The Mastodon bookmarks endpoint requires OAuth user-context authentication: a user token passed as a Bearer Authorization header, with the read:bookmarks OAuth scope — there is no additional cost or paid tier, just standard Mastodon OAuth.

The Semantic Scholar API is free to use, and most endpoints are publicly accessible without any authentication; an API key is optional and only certain endpoints require it, meaning a sandboxed macOS client can call it directly with no server-side secret and no OAuth flow.

Unauthenticated (keyless) access to the Semantic Scholar API is rate-limited to a shared pool of 1,000 requests per second across ALL unauthenticated users worldwide, so a client app without a key may be throttled during heavy global use.

An authenticated Semantic Scholar API key starts at a dedicated rate limit of 1 request per second on all endpoints; keys are private, distributed via email (simple API-key auth, not OAuth), and must not be shared — compatible with per-user Keychain storage in a client app.

Semantic Scholar allows unauthenticated (no API key) access to its public API, with all unauthenticated users sharing a pooled rate limit of 5,000 requests per 5 minutes (since March 28, 2023) — meaning a sandboxed Mac client can call the API with no key and no server, but throughput is unpredictable because the pool is shared globally across all unauthenticated users.

As of August 2024, Semantic Scholar stopped approving API key requests for third-party apps and for requests from free email domains — so Epistemos cannot ship or obtain an app-level S2 key, and individual users on gmail-type addresses cannot get personal keys either; the unauthenticated pool is effectively the only client-side path.

The Readwise Reader API uses simple static-token authentication (an 'Authorization: Token XXX' header) with each user obtaining their own token from readwise.io/access_token — there is no OAuth flow or app-registration program documented, and the docs explicitly anticipate third-party integrations directing 'your users' to fetch their own tokens, which means a sandboxed client-side-only Mac app can integrate with no server middleman and no embedded secret (user pastes token, app stores it in Keychain).

Readwise Reader API rate limits are per access token — 50 requests/minute for document CREATE (POST /save/) and UPDATE, and 20 requests/minute for LIST, DELETE, bulk update, and tag endpoints — and exceeding a limit returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header giving the seconds to wait, so a per-user feed poller stays comfortably inside limits.

The Reader API v3 (base URL https://readwise.io/api/v3/) exposes a full two-way surface — save/create document, list documents, update, bulk update, delete, and list tags — with cursor-based pagination (nextPageCursor) on the list endpoint, which is sufficient for both a 'save from Epistemos to Reader' action and a 'sync my Reader library/queue into the ResearchHub' adapter.
Raindrop.io provides an official, publicly documented API covering its service, hosted at developer.raindrop.io.

Third-party access to the Raindrop.io API requires registering an application and authenticating via OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow, and the token exchange (POST https://raindrop.io/oauth/access_token) requires a client_secret in the request body (parameters: grant_type, code, client_id, client_secret, redirect_uri), with no PKCE option documented — meaning a pure client-side distributed app cannot complete the flow without embedding a secret or using a server middleman.
